- If sentiment is consistently low or negative (≤ 0.2) in recent days, model should reduce forecast slope or avoid upward bias.  
- If model shows strong upward trend (e.g., >88.5) with sentiment neutral or positive, check for overshoot — cap forecast at 10% above recent peak if sentiment drops.  
- If true outcome shows sharp downward spike after model’s peak, model likely overestimated momentum — apply mean reversion correction by reducing forecast slope by 10–15% post-spike.  
- If sentiment is high (≥ 0.7) and model is flat or slightly rising, consider slight upward bias — allow 2–3% above recent mean if sentiment remains strong.  
- If model forecast is flat or slightly declining while sentiment is positive, model may be underestimating momentum — adjust upward by 1–2% per day if sentiment > 0.6.  
- If true outcome shows strong upward movement after model’s low, model may be underestimating rebound — increase forecast slope by 5–10% if sentiment > 0.5 and recent low is below 80.  
- Avoid forecasting above 95.0 if sentiment is negative or recent history shows volatility — cap at 95.0 if sentiment < 0.3.  
- If model forecast is above 90.0 and sentiment is neutral or negative, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overconfidence bias.  
- If sentiment is negative and model is rising, apply downward bias correction — reduce forecast by 3–5% per day if sentiment < 0.2.  
- If model forecast is below 80.0 and sentiment is positive, consider upward bias — increase forecast by 2–5% if sentiment > 0.6 and recent low is below 75.
